content: Electrocardiogram (EKG) artifacts are defined as abnormalities in the EKG tracing that are not related to the electrical activity of the heart. These artifacts can distort the normal components of the EKG, such as the P wave, QRS complex, T wave, and PR and ST segments. Recognizing these artifacts is crucial, as failure to do so can lead to unnecessary diagnostic tests and inappropriate therapeutic interventions. Causes of EKG Artifacts EKG artifacts can arise from both internal and external sources. Internal Causes 1. Patient Motion: Movements such as stretching of the skin (epidermal stretching) can produce large swings in the EKG tracing, which cannot be filtered electronically. Tremors and shivering are common causes of motion artifacts. Even simple activities like brushing or combing hair during ambulatory EKG monitoring can result in disturbances. 2. Muscular Activity: Muscle contractions can generate small spikes on the EKG tracing, which are often filtered electronically. External Causes 1. Medical Equipment: Artifacts can also be caused by issues with electrodes, leads, amplifiers, or filters. Identification of Artifacts Artifacts can distort individual or multiple components of the EKG. While they are often easily identifiable and dismissed because they do not resemble specific patterns, it is essential to differentiate these changes from genuine abnormalities to avoid misdiagnosis. For example: Artifacts affecting the ST segment can mimic ST segment depression or elevation, which may be misinterpreted as myocardial ischemia or infarction. Differentiating Artifacts from Ventricular Tachycardia EKG artifacts can sometimes mimic arrhythmias such as ventricular tachycardia, atrial flutter, or atrial fibrillation. Misdiagnosis in such cases can lead to inappropriate use of medications or procedures. Key characteristics that help differentiate artifacts from true ventricular tachycardia include: Absence of hemodynamic deterioration during the event. Presence of normal QRS complexes within the artifact. An unstable baseline on the EKG before, after, or during the event. Association with bodily movement. Huang et al. described three specific signs to distinguish tremor-induced pseudo-ventricular tachycardia from true ventricular tachycardia: 1. Sinus Sign: One of the frontal leads (I, II, or III) may show a normal sinus rhythm with intact P, QRS, and T waves. This occurs because one of the upper limbs may be free of tremor. 2. Spike Sign: Regular or irregular tiny spikes may appear among wide-QRS-like complexes. 3. Notch Sign: Notches superimposed on the wide-QRS-like artifact, coinciding with the cycle length of the recorded sinus rhythm. Electrode Misplacement Misplacement of electrodes is a common source of artifacts that can mimic life-threatening arrhythmias. Early identification and correction of electrode placement can prevent unnecessary therapies. Algorithms have been developed to help recognize these artifacts. Other Common Artifacts 1. Electrodes on the Torso: Placing electrodes on the torso instead of the limbs can alter the electrical vectors, producing pseudo-Q waves and pseudo-ST segment elevation, which may mimic myocardial infarction. 2. Telemetry Interference: Overlapping telemetry electrodes with EKG electrodes can cause ST segment deviations due to electromagnetic interference. 3. Loose Wires: A straight line may resemble systole, while a wavy line may mimic fibrillation. However, these artifacts are usually limited to one or two leads. 4. Tall T Waves: A tall T wave may be mistaken for an R wave, leading to an erroneously high digital heart rate compared to the actual pulse rate. 5. Lead Placement Issues: Improper lead placement can obscure P waves, mimicking heart block. 6. Motion Artifacts: Movements such as chest percussions or physiotherapy can mimic ventricular fibrillation. Consequences of EKG Artifacts Artifacts can lead to poor-quality EKG recordings and, more importantly, can mimic genuine abnormalities. If not recognized, they may result in unnecessary diagnostic and therapeutic measures, such as invasive investigations or administration of medications like antiarrhythmics. Correction of Artifacts 1. Attention to basic principles, such as proper electrode placement and lead connections, is essential during EKG monitoring. 2. Well-designed and well-maintained EKG devices can minimize routine disturbances caused by internal or external factors. However, complete elimination of artifacts is not always possible. 3. Physicians must remain vigilant and consider artifacts in their differential diagnosis when interpreting EKGs. Examples of Artifacts 1. Movement Artifacts: These are common in patients with movement disorders, such as Parkinson’s disease, and can increase with the severity of the movement. 2. Baseline Drift: This occurs when the EKG amplifier adjusts to find the mean after lead connection or electrical cardioversion. It is often seen after cardioversion from atrial fibrillation to sinus rhythm. 3. Electrical Interference: Nearby electrical appliances, such as fluorescent lights, can cause a 100 Hz background distortion. This should not be confused with atrial fibrillation. 4. Other Electrical Artifacts: For example, interference from an electrical appliance may produce a regular rhythm on the EKG, but the patient’s actual rhythm remains unaffected. By recognizing and addressing these artifacts, clinicians can avoid misinterpretation and ensure accurate diagnosis and treatment.
